lead: One processor cannot get much faster, so since the 1960s we buy more of them. Parallel computing puts many processors on one job and lets them share memory, so they cooperate cheaply. Distributed computing joins separate computers that share nothing but a network, so they must send messages. The cloud is the second kind — a distributed system of data-centre machines — wrapped in a business layer that rents them by the second, from an IRCTC tatkal surge to a startup's first server.
prereq: You need chapter 1.1 for the habit of pooling computers into clusters, grids and utilities.

sections.h3: Parallel versus distributed: the memory decides

blocks.text: Parallel computing is one job spread over several processors inside one machine. The processors share one memory, so a processor can leave a partial result in a variable and another processor reads it directly. That exchange costs nanoseconds. They also share one clock, one operating system and one power supply.

Distributed computing is several independent computers, each with its own memory, its own clock and often its own administrator, joined only by a network. To cooperate they send messages: a request goes out, a reply comes back. A message costs microseconds to milliseconds, thousands of times more than a memory read.

That cost forces a different design. A parallel program can rely on a lock in shared memory. A distributed program must tolerate a message that never arrives, a node that dies while the others keep running (partial failure), concurrent updates from users it does not control, and clocks that disagree by seconds. No global clock means you cannot order two events on different machines by their timestamps alone.

blocks.text: The two are used together: a cloud data centre is a distributed system whose individual nodes are multicore parallel machines. The transparency a distributed system promises — you see one service, not a hundred servers — is what the cloud then sells.

Flynn classified machines by how many instruction streams and data streams they handle at once. An instruction stream is the sequence of operations a processor executes; a data stream is the set of operands those operations touch. Some syllabi call this the classification of parallel systems.

items: SISD — single instruction, single data. One core working through one array. A basic laptop.
SIMD — single instruction, multiple data. One add applied to 32 numbers at once. A GPU, a vector unit, a CPU's SSE lane.
MISD — multiple instruction, single data. Several processors act on the same data. Almost no commercial machine; systolic arrays and triple-redundant flight computers are the textbook examples.
MIMD — multiple instruction, multiple data. Independent cores running independent code. A multicore server, a cluster, the cloud itself.

blocks.text: MIMD splits again by how the processors talk. In shared memory they read and write one address space and synchronise with locks. In message passing each has private memory and calls send and receive, so the programmer must move data explicitly. The cores inside one cloud server are shared memory; the servers inside one rack are message passing. The interconnection network — the bus, the crossbar switch or the data-centre fabric — decides how fast either can be.

sections.h3: Amdahl's law: the serial part sets the bill

blocks.text: Split a job into a fraction p that can run in parallel and a fraction 1 − p that cannot: reading the input, a final merge, a sequential loop. With n processors the best possible speedup is bounded by Amdahl's law.

blocks.where: S is the speedup (serial time ÷ parallel time, a pure ratio), p is the fraction of the work that can run in parallel (0 to 1), n is the number of processors, and 1 − p is the serial fraction. It assumes perfect load balance and zero communication cost.

blocks.text: As n grows, p/n shrinks to zero and S stops at the ceiling 1/(1 − p). That is the serial fraction's revenge: p = 0.95 caps you at 20×, p = 0.90 at 10×, p = 0.75 at 4×.

The same arithmetic decides what to parallelise in a cloud. Task parallelism gives different tasks to different servers — 200 product pages rendered at once. Data parallelism splits one dataset into chunks — a 500 GB log file into 200 blocks, each counted by one worker — the same shape as SIMD, one operation over many data items. The programming models for both are in Unit 5.

items: Batch mainframe, 1950s–60s. One costly machine in a locked room. Jobs on punched cards, results the next morning. Processing is central and users queue.
Time-sharing, 1960s–70s. Terminals hang off one mainframe, each user gets a time slice and works interactively. The pool is shared and billed by connect time.
Personal computer, 1980s. One user per machine. Cheap and private, but idle most of the day and owned by the user.
Client-server and the web, 1990s. The application sits on the desktop, data and logic on a server; then the browser becomes the client and server farms grow behind it.
Cloud and mobile, 2000s onwards. Computing returns to a shared pool, now metered per second and elastic. The phone and browser are terminals again, and the pool belongs to someone else.

blocks.text: The shape is central, then decentralised, then central again — but the new centre is rented, not owned. That is why the parallel-versus-distributed distinction matters commercially: a provider amortises one distributed data centre over thousands of tenants, and a tenant gets parallelism on demand without buying a machine. Chapter 1.3 turns this into a test.

examples.question: A batch job has 80% of its work that can run in parallel, so p = 0.8. Find the speedup on n = 4, n = 16 and n = 1000 processors, and state the maximum speedup any number of processors could give.
steps: Serial fraction: 1 − p = 1 − 0.8 = 0.2. This part runs on one processor whatever n is.
n = 4: p/n = 0.8/4 = 0.2, so the denominator is 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4 and S = 1/0.4 = 2.5.
examples.answer: Speedups of 2.5×, 4.0× and about 4.98×, with a hard ceiling of 5× however many processors are bought.
examples.check:
p = 0.8
for n in [4, 16, 1000]:
    s = 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)
    print(round(s, 2))
print(round(1 / (1 - p), 2))

traps: Writing n as the number of tasks or threads instead of the number of processors. Amdahl's n is processors.
Forgetting the ceiling 1/(1 − p) and claiming speedup keeps growing; no answer above n is possible without superlinear effects from cache, which the model ignores.
Answering 'many machines' for parallel versus distributed. The real differences are shared memory versus a network, and one clock versus no global clock.
Treating MISD as a real machine class. It is theoretical; the ones you meet are SISD, SIMD and MIMD.
Using total time in Amdahl's law instead of the parallel fraction p. Convert first: p = parallel time ÷ total serial time.

quiz.q: Define parallel computing and distributed computing in one line each.
quiz.a: Parallel: many processors in one machine share memory and one clock to run one job. Distributed: independent computers with private memory and no shared clock cooperate by passing messages over a network.

quiz.q: Name Flynn's four classes and give one example of each.
quiz.a: SISD — single-core laptop. SIMD — GPU or vector unit. MISD — systolic array (theoretical). MIMD — multicore server or cloud cluster.

quiz.q: Why can a distributed system not use timestamps alone to order two events?
quiz.a: Each machine has its own clock and the clocks drift apart by seconds. There is no global clock, so ordering needs logical clocks, sequence numbers or message causality.

quiz.q: Why does message passing cost far more than a shared-memory read?
quiz.a: A shared read is a load instruction to local memory, nanoseconds. A message is copied into a network stack, crosses a switch or cable, and is copied out on the far side: microseconds to milliseconds, plus possible loss.

quiz.q: A job is 90% parallelisable. Find the speedup on 8 processors and the ceiling.
A job is 60% parallelisable with 10 processors. Compute the speedup and the fraction of time still spent serial.
quiz.a: p/n = 0.6/10 = 0.06. Denominator 0.4 + 0.06 = 0.46. S = 1/0.46 ≈ 2.17×. Serial share of parallel time = 0.4/0.46 ≈ 87%.

quiz.q: With p = 0.9, going from 32 to 64 processors adds little speedup. Explain using Amdahl's law.
quiz.a: S(32) = 1/(0.1 + 0.028125) ≈ 7.80 and S(64) = 1/(0.1 + 0.0140625) ≈ 8.77. Doubling processors gains about 0.97× because the 0.1 serial part dominates the denominator; the ceiling is 10×.

quiz.q: A team says: 'We moved the app to many servers, so speedup is now unlimited.' Refute this in terms of the chapter.
quiz.a: Going distributed adds network messages and partial failure, which raise the serial and coordination cost. Amdahl's law still applies and its ceiling falls as the serial fraction rises, so more servers can make it slower, not unbounded.

beyond: Not for the exam. Amdahl's law gets its practical partner in Gustafson's law, which asks how large a problem you can finish in fixed time as processors grow rather than how fast one fixed problem runs. Real clouds are judged by the tail latency of the slowest of hundreds of parallel sub-requests, which is why providers engineer for p99 and not the mean. Modern data-centre fabrics and remote direct memory access push message costs towards memory costs, blurring the shared-memory and message-passing line. Search for Gustafson's law, tail latency in microservices, and remote direct memory access.
